items.name: Vacuuming old row versions
items.explanation: When a database keeps old versions of a row so readers are not blocked, something has to clear them out later. Vacuuming is that clean-up, and it frees the space for reuse.

assumedBy.quote: By comparison, the Postgres autovacuum process has to do full table scans to identify deleted rows.

items.name: The operating system page cache
items.explanation: The operating system keeps recently read file data in memory, in the page cache, so a repeat read skips the disk. A database can lean on it or keep a cache of its own.

assumedBy.quote: To increase performance, Postgres allows the kernel to automatically cache recently accessed disk data via the page cache.

items.diagram: <svg viewBox="0 0 560 110" role="img" aria-labelledby="dg-db-bg-pc-t" class="dg"><title id="dg-db-bg-pc-t">A read checks the operating system page cache in memory first; only when the data is not there does it go to disk.</title><defs><marker id="dg-db-bg-pc-a" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="8" markerHeight="8" orient="auto-start-reverse"><path d="M1,1 L9,5 L1,9" class="dg-head"/></marker></defs><rect x="14" y="10" width="100" height="44" class="dg-box"/><text x="64" y="36.55" class="dg-label" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13">Read</text><rect x="180" y="10" width="140" height="44" class="dg-box dg-accent"/><text x="250" y="28.55" class="dg-label" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13">Page cache</text><text x="250" y="44.55" class="dg-label" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13">in memory</text><rect x="440" y="10" width="106" height="44" class="dg-box"/><text x="493" y="36.55" class="dg-label" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13">Data back</text><path d="M114,32 L180,32" class="dg-line" marker-end="url(#dg-db-bg-pc-a)"/><path d="M320,32 L440,32" class="dg-line" marker-end="url(#dg-db-bg-pc-a)"/><text x="380" y="24" class="dg-note" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11">repeat read</text><path d="M250,54 L250,70" class="dg-line" marker-end="url(#dg-db-bg-pc-a)"/><text x="260" y="66" class="dg-note" text-anchor="start" font-size="11">not there</text><rect x="180" y="70" width="140" height="34" class="dg-box"/><text x="250" y="91.55" class="dg-label" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13">Disk</text></svg>

items.name: Connection pooling
items.explanation: A pooler sits between the applications and the database and reuses a limited set of real connections. In transaction pooling a server connection is lent to a client only for one transaction.

assumedBy.quote: While the documentation is not very specific about why, it does strongly recommend employing an out-of-process connection pooling mechanism to scale to large connection counts with Postgres.

items.diagram: <svg viewBox="0 0 560 100" role="img" aria-labelledby="dg-db-bg-cp-t" class="dg"><title id="dg-db-bg-cp-t">A pooler sits between applications and the database and reuses a limited set of real connections.</title><defs><marker id="dg-db-bg-cp-a" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="8" markerHeight="8" orient="auto-start-reverse"><path d="M1,1 L9,5 L1,9" class="dg-head"/></marker></defs><rect x="14" y="16" width="140" height="50" class="dg-box"/><text x="84" y="37.55" class="dg-label" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13">Applications</text><text x="84" y="53.55" class="dg-label" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13">many clients</text><rect x="195.0" y="16" width="170" height="50" class="dg-box dg-accent"/><text x="280" y="37.55" class="dg-label" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13">Pooler</text><text x="280" y="53.55" class="dg-label" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13">reuses connections</text><rect x="406.0" y="16" width="140" height="50" class="dg-box"/><text x="476" y="37.55" class="dg-label" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13">Database</text><text x="476" y="53.55" class="dg-label" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13">real connections</text><path d="M154,41 L195,41" class="dg-line" marker-end="url(#dg-db-bg-cp-a)"/><path d="M365,41 L406,41" class="dg-line" marker-end="url(#dg-db-bg-cp-a)"/><text x="280" y="92" class="dg-note" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11">a server connection is lent out, then reused</text></svg>

items.name: Service level objectives (SLOs)
items.explanation: An SLO is a target for how a service should behave, such as the share of requests that succeed or finish fast enough. A team plans every change, even a long upgrade, to stay inside it.

assumedBy.quote: We must be able to upgrade each MySQL database while adhering to our Service Level Objectives (SLOs) and Service Level Agreements (SLAs).

sources.title: Service Level Objectives (Site Reliability Engineering, chapter 4)

items.name: B-tree indexes
items.explanation: A sorted tree of keys that lets the database find a row, or a range of rows, without reading the whole table.

assumedBy.quote: Tables themselves have indexes, which are organized as data structures (typically B-trees) that map index fields to a ctid payload.

items.name: Sharding and shard keys
items.explanation: Splitting one big dataset across many databases by a key, so each holds only part of it.

assumedBy.quote: Specifically, in many of the cases where we previously used Postgres, we now use Schemaless, a novel database sharding layer built on top of MySQL.
We use Vitess for horizontally sharding relational data.

items.name: Promoting a replica
items.explanation: Making a replica the new primary, so the other copies follow it and writes keep flowing.

assumedBy.quote: During a routine master database promotion to increase database capacity, we ran into a Postgres 9.2 bug.
Instead, we would promote a MySQL 8.0 replica to primary through a graceful failover performed with Orchestrator.

items.name: Failover
items.explanation: Switching to another copy when the primary is lost, so writes can continue.

assumedBy.quote: Orchestrator was also configured to blacklist 5.7 hosts as potential failover candidates to prevent an accidental rollback in case of an unplanned failover.
